Shekel
SHEK-ul
n.
Hebrew sheqel, “weight,” from the verb shāqal, “to weigh.” The shekel was originally a unit of weight (approximately 0.4 oz / 11.4 g of silver) before becoming a coin; the Hebrew word means literally that-which-is-weighed.

📖 Biblical Definition

The shekel is the central unit of weight and currency across the Old Testament, the standard against which other weights and values were measured. Several shekels are distinguished in Scripture. The shekel of the sanctuary (Ex 30:13; 38:24-29) was the temple-standard, used for sacred dues including the half-shekel atonement tax every adult Israelite male paid for the support of the tabernacle service (Ex 30:11-16); twenty gerahs made one shekel of the sanctuary. The king’s shekel (2 Sam 14:26) may have been a different standard for royal weights. The shekel functioned as both weight (for measuring grain, metal, and other commodities) and currency (Abraham’s 400 shekels for the cave of Machpelah, Gen 23:15-16; Joseph sold for 20 shekels of silver, Gen 37:28; Judah’s pledge of a kid, his signet, bracelets, and staff in Gen 38; the bride-price of 50 shekels, Deut 22:29; David’s 50 shekels of silver and an ox-yoke for Araunah’s threshingfloor, 2 Sam 24:24; and the betrayal-price of 30 shekels of silver, Zech 11:12-13 prophetically and Matt 26:15 in fulfillment). The biblical pattern uses the shekel structurally across several theological-and-practical categories. Atonement: every adult Israelite paid a half-shekel for the sanctuary’s service, a token of the ransom by which the soul was kept from being numbered without redemption—a typological anticipation of the full ransom Christ would later pay. Land transactions: significant covenantal land purchases (Abraham’s field, David’s threshingfloor, Jeremiah’s field in chapter 32 as the prophetic sign of God’s coming restoration) are recorded in shekels, anchoring the covenantal land-promise in concrete commerce. Slavery and redemption: the price of a Hebrew slave, the bride-price of a virgin, the value placed on a person dedicated to the LORD (Lev 27)—all are measured in shekels. Betrayal: the 30 shekels of silver Judas received for delivering Christ to the chief priests is the price-tag pre-prophesied in Zechariah 11 of the despised Shepherd, and the fact that it is exactly the price of a slave gored by an ox (Ex 21:32) is the bitterly precise valuation human treachery placed on the Son of God incarnate. The shekel therefore is no merely numismatic curiosity but a structural unit of biblical economics, atonement-doctrine, covenantal land-theology, and the prophetic specification by which the betrayal of Christ is shown to fulfill the Old Testament word.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SHEKEL as an ancient weight and coin among the Jews, computed at half an ounce or about thirty cents in silver; the central OT unit of weight and currency, used for atonement, land transactions, slavery and redemption pricing, and the prophetic 30 shekels of Christ’s betrayal.

SHEKEL, n. — An ancient weight and coin among the Jews, computed at half an ounce. According to Calmet, the value was equal to 60 cents; according to other authors, it was about half a crown sterling, or 30 cents. The shekel is twenty gerahs (Ex 30:13).

WEIGHT, n. — That property of bodies by which they tend toward the center of the earth, in proportion to their quantity of matter; a quality measured by the balance and the standard weights.

📖 Key Scripture

Exodus 30:13 — "This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD."

Genesis 23:15-16 — "My lord, hearken unto me: the land is worth four hundred shekels of silver; what is that betwixt me and thee? bury therefore thy dead. And Abraham hearkened unto Ephron; and Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant."

Zechariah 11:12-13 — "And I said unto them, If ye think good, give me my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver. And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD."

Matthew 26:14-15 — "Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went unto the chief priests, And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The shekel as a biblical unit is corrupted in modern reading chiefly by being treated as a mere historical-numismatic curiosity rather than as a structural unit of biblical atonement-doctrine, covenantal land-theology, and prophetic Christology; recovery requires reading the shekel-weighted transactions as the theological substance they are.

expand to see more

The contemporary reader, faced with the shekels of Scripture, tends to treat them as ancient currency-curiosities, looking up the modern dollar-equivalent and moving on. The biblical writers used the shekel structurally, and several theological doctrines are tied directly to specific shekel-weighted transactions: the half-shekel of the sanctuary anchors the doctrine of atonement-as-ransom, anticipating the full ransom Christ would pay; Abraham’s 400 shekels for the cave of Machpelah anchor the covenantal land-promise in concrete legal-commercial transaction; David’s 50 shekels for Araunah’s threshingfloor anchor the temple-site in his refusal to offer to God that which cost him nothing; the 30 shekels of Christ’s betrayal anchor the prophetic Zech 11 specification in concrete historical fulfillment. To read past the shekel-figures is to miss the precision with which Scripture has tied its great doctrines to concrete commercial reality.

The supreme case is the 30 shekels of silver paid to Judas. The figure is not arbitrary. Exodus 21:32 specifies 30 shekels as the price of a slave gored by an ox—the basement price of an expendable life. Zechariah 11:12-13 prophetically sets the price at which the despised Shepherd was valued, with the dramatic instruction to cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them. Matthew 27:9-10 reports the fulfillment in the precise detail: Judas casts the silver in the temple, the priests use it to buy the potter’s field, and the prophet’s word is fulfilled. The price-tag on Christ’s body delivered to His enemies was exactly the price-tag on a slave gored by an ox: the basement valuation of an expendable life, paid by the religious establishment to a faithless friend, fulfilling the prophetic word given centuries before. The contemporary reader who has skipped past 30 shekels of silver as a quaint historical detail has missed one of the most precise prophetic-Christological connections in the entire Bible. Recover the shekel-precision, and recover the doctrinal substance the precision conveys.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sheqel (weight; the central OT unit of weight and currency) from shāqal (to weigh)—structural to OT economics, the half-shekel atonement tax, covenantal land transactions, slavery-and-redemption pricing, and the prophetic 30 shekels of Christ’s betrayal.

expand to see more

Hebrew sheqel (H8255) — shekel (weight, currency).

Hebrew shāqal (H8254) — to weigh (the etymological verb).

Hebrew gerah (H1626) — gerah (smaller weight; 20 gerahs = 1 shekel of the sanctuary).

Greek argurion (G694) — piece of silver (NT term for the 30 silver pieces of Judas; Matt 26:15).

"The 30 shekels of Christ’s betrayal is exactly the price of a slave gored by an ox (Ex 21:32) and the precise fulfillment of Zech 11:12-13—the basement valuation of an expendable life, placed by men on the Son of God."
